blogs.title: Navigating Mixed Motives: The Nexus Requirement and the 'Central Reason' Test
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Tenth Circuit’s treatment of the 'nexus' requirement in asylum law. It explores how the court distinguished between the petitioners' political affiliation and the specific professional actions of the lead petitioner. Specifically, it discusses the legal implications of the court finding that the motive for persecution was 'tangential' to political opinion, focusing on the 'central reason' standard in cases involving mixed motives of personal vendetta and political activity.

blogs.title: The Persecution Threshold: Distinguishing 'Unfortunate Circumstances' from Legal Persecution
blogs.description: This post examines the evidentiary bar for establishing 'past persecution' under the INA. It analyzes the court's reasoning that cumulative threats and psychological distress—while 'physically stressful and psychologically unsettling'—do not necessarily reach the legal threshold of persecution. The post will discuss the tension between the subjective experience of the asylum seeker and the court’s objective, often restrictive, definition of what constitutes 'offensive' harm.

blogs.title: The Reporting Requirement and the 'Unable or Unwilling' Analysis
blogs.description: Focusing on the government protection prong, this post explores the court's skepticism toward asylum claims where the applicant failed to report persecution to the authorities. It analyzes the court's distinction between 'systemic' government failure and 'one-off' interactions with individual police officers, and the significant hurdles this creates for applicants who fear that reporting is futile or dangerous.

blogs.title: Internal Relocation: Practical Geography vs. Systemic Infrastructure
blogs.description: This post looks at the final hurdle of asylum: the reasonableness of internal relocation. It contrasts the petitioners' arguments regarding the country's crumbling judicial infrastructure and political ties with the court's more localized, practical finding that relocation to the countryside was feasible. The post will discuss the broader trend of how courts weigh administrative/economic burdens against geographic safety.
